word: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
etymology: From the Old English fedan, “to give food,” naming the miracle in which Christ fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes.
biblical_def: The feeding of the five thousand is the only one of Christ’s miracles recorded in all four Gospels, a sign of His almighty power and a witness to His Person. When the day was far spent in a desert place, the disciples would have sent the multitude away to buy victuals; but Jesus said, They need not depart; give ye them to eat (Mat 14:16). There were but five loaves and two fishes; yet He took them, and looking up to heaven, He blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to His disciples (Mat 14:19). They did all eat, and were filled, five thousand men beside women and children, and they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments (Mat 14:20). The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for none but the Creator can multiply bread out of His own hand; and as a sign of His Messianic office, for He is the Shepherd who feeds His flock in the wilderness. The LORD drew out the meaning Himself when He preached at Capernaum: I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger (Joh 6:35). The loaves that perished pointed to the bread that endureth unto everlasting life, even His own flesh given for the world; and the satisfied multitude is a figure of the elect, fed to the full by the Saviour who is Himself their food.
webster_summary: The miracle in which Christ fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, a sign of His deity as the Bread of life.
webster_full: THE FEEDING OF THE FIVE THOUSAND, the miracle in which Christ fed a multitude with five loaves and two fishes.
It is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.
He blessed and brake the loaves, and all did eat and were filled.
Twelve baskets of fragments remained after five thousand men were fed.
It is a sign of Christ the Bread of life, who satisfies His people forever.
scriptures: And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.
And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full.
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Joh 6:14
Then those men, when they had seen the miracle that Jesus did, said, This is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; chiefly assailed by the modern denial of the miraculous itself, which the eyewitness record and Christ’s deity refute.
corruption_paragraphs: The feeding of the five thousand has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for the Gospels are plain that it sets forth Christ the Bread of life. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark both the miracle and the sermon the LORD built upon it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The one assault it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would explain the miracle away as a tale of men sharing their own provisions, or as a legend grown in the telling. But this is the anti-supernatural prejudice imposed upon the text, not drawn from it; the four evangelists, eyewitnesses or the recorders of eyewitnesses, declare a true multiplication of bread by the hand of God incarnate. He who made the worlds can multiply five loaves; and the principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity and His Messianic office as the Shepherd who feeds His flock, satisfying forever the souls that come to Him.
roots_summary: The miracle of the loaves and fishes, by which Christ proved Himself the Bread of life come down from heaven.
roots_lines: The Feeding of the Five Thousand — Christ’s miracle of multiplying five loaves and two fishes.
It is recorded in all four Gospels.
He blessed and brake the loaves, and all were filled.
Twelve baskets of fragments remained over.
It signs forth Christ the Bread of life, who never leaves His own to hunger.
usage: As at the feeding of the five thousand, Christ takes the little His people bring and multiplies it for the good of many.
I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger.
The loaves that perished pointed to the bread that endureth unto everlasting life.

word: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
etymology: From the Old English fedan, “to give food,” naming the second feeding miracle, in which Christ fed four thousand with seven loaves and a few fishes.
biblical_def: The feeding of the four thousand is the second of Christ’s great provision miracles, distinct from the feeding of the five thousand and recorded by Matthew and Mark. The multitude had been with Him three days in the wilderness and had nothing to eat, and the LORD was moved with compassion, saying, I will not send them away fasting, lest they faint in the way (Mat 15:32). There were seven loaves and a few little fishes; and He took them, and gave thanks, and brake, and gave to His disciples, and the disciples to the multitude (Mat 15:36). They did all eat, and were filled, four thousand men beside women and children, and they took up seven baskets full of the broken meat that was left (Mat 15:37). The dictionary marks this second feeding as a renewed sign of Christ’s true deity, for the multiplication of bread is a work of the Creator alone; and of His Messianic office, for the bread of the wilderness is His to give. Afterward the LORD rebuked His disciples for their slowness of heart, that they remembered neither the five loaves of the five thousand nor the seven loaves of the four thousand. So the two feedings stand as a double witness, that He who fed Israel with manna in the desert was now present in the flesh, the very Bread of God come down to feed His people.
webster_summary: The second feeding miracle, in which Christ fed four thousand men with seven loaves and a few fishes.
webster_full: THE FEEDING OF THE FOUR THOUSAND, the second miracle in which Christ fed a multitude in the wilderness.
The people had been with Him three days and had nothing to eat.
He gave thanks and brake seven loaves and a few little fishes.
Four thousand men were filled, and seven baskets of fragments remained.
It is a second sign of His deity, distinct from the feeding of the five thousand.
scriptures: Then Jesus called his disciples unto him, and said, I have compassion on the multitude, because they continue with me now three days, and have nothing to eat: and I will not send them away fasting, lest they faint in the way.
And he took the seven loaves and the fishes, and gave thanks, and brake them, and gave to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.
And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the broken meat that was left seven baskets full.
Mar 8:19
When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the modern denial of the miraculous, and sometimes wrongly merged into the first feeding.
corruption_paragraphs: The feeding of the four thousand has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, though some have wrongly supposed it but a doubled telling of the first feeding. The dictionary records it as the distinct second miracle the Gospels plainly set apart by their numbers, that the reader may mark Christ’s repeated witness to His own power.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the two feedings are a double witness to Christ’s deity and His office as the Bread of life. The LORD Himself distinguished them, asking His disciples how many baskets remained from the five loaves and how many from the seven; and He chid their dulness for forgetting either. He who fed Israel with manna fed these multitudes with multiplied bread; and the compassion that would not send the fainting away unfed is the same compassion that feeds the souls of His elect, that they faint not in the way to the kingdom.
roots_summary: The second feeding miracle, a renewed sign that Christ is the Creator and the Bread of God in the flesh.
roots_lines: The Feeding of the Four Thousand — Christ’s second multiplying of loaves and fishes.
It is recorded by Matthew and Mark.
He fed four thousand men with seven loaves and a few fishes.
Seven baskets of fragments remained over.
It stands with the first feeding as a double witness to His deity.
usage: As at the feeding of the four thousand, the compassion of Christ will not send His fainting people away unfed.
I have compassion on the multitude, because they continue with me now three days.
In the mouth of two feeding miracles the witness to His deity is established.

etymology: From the Latin vinum, “wine,” naming Christ’s first miracle, the turning of water into wine at the marriage in Cana of Galilee.
biblical_def: The turning of water into wine at the marriage in Cana of Galilee was the first of Christ’s miracles, the beginning of His signs. When the wine failed at the feast, His mother told Him; and when she had said to the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it (Joh 2:5), He bade them fill the six waterpots of stone with water, and they filled them to the brim. Then He said, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast; and the water that was made wine was found better than that served first, so that the governor marvelled. The dictionary marks this as the first manifestation of Christ’s glory, the opening sign of His ministry. For the evangelist says plainly, This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him (Joh 2:11). None but the Creator, who made the vine and gives the fruit thereof, could in a moment turn water into the best of wine without the slow working of root and grape and press; the miracle therefore signs forth His true deity. It signs forth also His Messianic office, for the prophets foretold that in the days of the Messiah the mountains should drop sweet wine. So the LORD, who came eating and drinking, hallowed the marriage covenant by His presence, and showed Himself the Lord of the new wine of the kingdom, the Bridegroom come to His own.
webster_summary: Christ’s first miracle, the turning of water into wine at Cana, whereby He manifested forth His glory.
webster_full: THE WATER MADE WINE, Christ’s first miracle, wrought at the marriage in Cana of Galilee.
When the wine failed, He bade the servants fill six waterpots with water.
The water was made wine, better than that first served at the feast.
It was the beginning of His miracles and manifested forth His glory.
His disciples saw it and believed on Him.
scriptures: Joh 2:7
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
Joh 2:9
When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,
Joh 2:11
This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.
Joh 2:5
His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the anti-supernatural denial of the miraculous, which the evangelist’s witness refutes.
corruption_paragraphs: The turning of water into wine has drawn little redefinition, for John names it plainly the beginning of miracles and the manifesting of Christ’s glory. The dictionary records it as the opening sign by which the disciples were brought to believe on Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Such corruption as it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, the anti-supernatural assumption that no man can turn water into wine and therefore the account must be a parable or an embellishment. But John was there, and he sets the sign down as a true work and the foundation of the disciples’ faith; this beginning of miracles manifested forth His glory, and his disciples believed on him. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, for only the Creator of the vine can make wine without the vine, and a sign of His Messianic office as the Bridegroom and the Lord of the kingdom’s new wine.
roots_summary: Christ’s first sign at Cana, by which He manifested His glory and confirmed His disciples’ faith.
roots_lines: The Water Made Wine — Christ’s first miracle at the marriage in Cana.
He bade the servants fill six waterpots with water.
The water was made the best wine of the feast.
It was the beginning of His miracles.
It manifested forth His glory, and His disciples believed on Him.
usage: As at Cana He made the water wine, so Christ still turns the want of His people into abundance.
This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth His glory.
Whatsoever He saith unto you, do it; for He is the Lord of the new wine of the kingdom.

etymology: From the Old English dragan, “to draw,” a draught being the taking of fish in a net, here the miraculous catch granted by Christ.
biblical_def: The miraculous draught of fishes was the sign by which Christ called Peter and the sons of Zebedee to be fishers of men. They had toiled all the night and taken nothing; but at His word, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught (Luk 5:4), they enclosed a great multitude of fishes, so that their net brake. Simon Peter, smitten with the sense of the holy presence, fell at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luk 5:8). And Jesus said, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men (Luk 5:10). The dictionary marks this draught as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for the fish of the sea are under His command, and the same Lord who said Let the waters bring forth abundantly now filled the empty nets at His word. It signs forth also the gathering of the church through the gospel; the empty night of unbelieving labour, and the full net at the bidding of Christ, set forth that no soul is caught for the kingdom but by His power. A second draught was granted after the resurrection, when the disciples drew their net to land full of great fishes, and yet it was not broken. So the LORD, the master of the sea, makes His servants fishers of men, and gathers His elect into the net of the gospel by His own almighty hand.
webster_summary: Christ’s miracle of the great catch of fishes, by which He called His disciples to be fishers of men.
webster_full: THE DRAUGHT OF FISHES, Christ’s miracle of the great catch granted to Peter and his partners.
They had toiled all night and taken nothing.
At His word they let down the net and enclosed a great multitude of fishes.
Peter fell at His knees, owning himself a sinful man.
Christ said, From henceforth thou shalt catch men.

corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the modern denial of the miraculous, which the disciples’ own witness refutes.
corruption_paragraphs: The miraculous draught of fishes has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for the Gospels are plain that it was the sign by which Christ called His first apostles. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark its sign-value for the gathering of the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is only the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would call the catch a lucky chance rather than a work of God. But Peter knew better, and fell at the Lord’s knees confessing himself a sinful man, for he discerned the holy power that filled the net at a word. The principle to recover is that the draught is a sign of Christ’s true deity, the Lord of the sea and its creatures, and a sign of His Messianic office in the gathering of the elect; for the empty night and the full net teach that the church is built not by the labour of man but by the power of Christ, who makes His servants fishers of men.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle of the great catch, a sign of His deity and of the gospel-gathering of His church.
roots_lines: The Draught of Fishes — Christ’s miracle of the great catch of fishes.
The disciples had toiled all night and taken nothing.
At His word the net enclosed a great multitude of fishes.
Peter owned himself a sinful man before the holy presence.
A second draught was granted after the resurrection.
usage: As at the draught of fishes, the church is gathered not by man’s labour but at the word of Christ.
Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.

etymology: From the Old English wealcan, “to roll” or “to move about,” naming the miracle in which Christ walked upon the sea to His disciples.
biblical_def: The walking upon the water was the miracle in which Christ came to His disciples in the fourth watch of the night, treading the waves of the sea as upon dry land. The ship was tossed with waves, for the wind was contrary; and Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea (Mat 14:25). They were troubled, supposing it had been a spirit, but He said, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid (Mat 14:27). Peter, bidden to come, walked on the water to go to Jesus; but when he saw the wind boisterous he was afraid, and beginning to sink, cried, Lord, save me; and immediately Jesus stretched forth His hand and caught him. When they were come into the ship, the wind ceased. The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for the LORD alone treadeth upon the waves of the sea (Job 9:8), and He who made the waters bore Himself upon them at His pleasure. The men in the ship discerned it, and came and worshipped Him, saying, Of a truth thou art the Son of God (Mat 14:33). So the miracle is a sign of His Messianic office and very Godhead; and it teaches that Christ is sovereign over the storm, comes to His own in the dark watches of trouble, and stretches forth His hand to catch the sinking saint whose eye leaves Him for the boisterous wind.
webster_summary: The miracle in which Christ walked upon the sea to His disciples, proving Himself the Son of God.
webster_full: WALKING ON THE WATER, the miracle in which Christ came to His disciples walking on the sea.
He came in the fourth watch of the night, the ship being tossed with waves.
He said, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
Peter walked on the water but began to sink, and Christ caught him.
They worshipped Him, saying, Of a truth thou art the Son of God.
scriptures: And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.
But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
Then they that were in the ship came and worshipped him, saying, Of a truth thou art the Son of God.
Job 9:8
Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the anti-supernatural denial of the miraculous, which the worship of the disciples refutes.
corruption_paragraphs: The walking upon the water has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for Matthew records it as the sign that drew from the disciples the confession of Christ as the Son of God. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark its plain witness to His deity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would have Christ walking on a sandbar or on the shore mistaken for the sea. But the text says He came to them in the midst of the sea, in the fourth watch, the ship tossed with waves; and the men, beholding it, worshipped Him as the Son of God. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, for the LORD alone treadeth upon the waves of the sea, and a sign of His Messianic office; it teaches the church that Christ is sovereign over every storm, comes to His own in the dark, and stretches forth His hand to catch the sinking saint whose faith would fail.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle of treading the sea, a sign that drew the confession, Of a truth thou art the Son of God.
roots_lines: Walking on the Water — Christ’s miracle of treading upon the sea.
He came to His disciples in the fourth watch of the night.
He said, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
Peter walked on the water, then began to sink and was caught.
The disciples worshipped Him as the Son of God.
usage: As when He walked upon the water, Christ comes to His own in the dark watches of trouble.
Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
Of a truth thou art the Son of God, said they that saw Him tread the sea.

etymology: From the Latin tempestas, “storm” or “season,” naming the miracle in which Christ rebuked the wind and the sea and made a great calm.
biblical_def: The stilling of the tempest was the miracle in which Christ, asleep in the hinder part of the ship, rose at the cry of His disciples and commanded the storm to cease. There arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full; but He was asleep on a pillow, and they awoke Him, saying, Master, carest thou not that we perish? (Mar 4:38). And He arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm (Mar 4:39). The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for it is the LORD who maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still (Psa 107:29), and none but the Creator of wind and sea can command them with a word. The disciples were driven to the right question, for they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mar 4:41). The answer is that He is no mere man, but the Son of God in our flesh, Lord of the elements He made. So the miracle teaches the church that Christ is never truly asleep to His people’s peril, that His word rules every tempest, and that the storms of providence cannot sink the ship that bears the Lord of the sea.
webster_summary: Christ’s miracle of rebuking the storm with a word, proving His command over wind and sea.
webster_full: THE STILLING OF THE TEMPEST, Christ’s miracle of calming the storm on the sea of Galilee.
A great storm arose while He slept in the hinder part of the ship.
The disciples woke Him, fearing they should perish.
He rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace, be still.
The wind ceased and there was a great calm.

Mar 4:39

He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the modern denial of the miraculous, which the disciples’ own astonishment refutes.
corruption_paragraphs: The stilling of the tempest has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for Mark records it as the sign that drove the disciples to ask what manner of man could command the sea. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark its witness to Christ’s deity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is only the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would have the storm subside of itself by natural chance just as Christ chanced to speak. But the evangelist sets word and calm together, that He rebuked the wind and the sea, and immediately there was a great calm; and the men feared exceedingly at it. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, for it is the LORD who maketh the storm a calm, and a sign of His Messianic office; it teaches that He is never truly asleep to His people’s peril, and that no tempest of providence can sink the ship that bears the Lord of wind and sea.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle of calming the storm, by which He proved Himself Lord of the wind and the sea.
roots_lines: The Stilling of the Tempest — Christ’s miracle of calming the storm with a word.
A great storm arose while He slept in the ship.
He rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace, be still.
The wind ceased and there was a great calm.
The disciples asked, What manner of man is this?
usage: As when He stilled the tempest, Christ speaks His Peace, be still, over the storms of His people.
He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?

etymology: From the Old English fic, after the Latin ficus, “fig,” naming the tree Christ cursed for its fruitlessness, which then withered away.
biblical_def: The withering of the fig tree was the one miracle of judgment among Christ’s works, wrought in the last week before His passion. Hungry as He came from Bethany, He saw a fig tree afar off having leaves, but found nothing thereon but leaves only; and He said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away (Mat 21:19). On the morrow the disciples marvelled how soon it was dried up from the roots (Mar 11:20). The dictionary marks this miracle as an acted parable of judgment upon barren profession. The tree that bore leaves but no fruit is a figure of Israel after the flesh, and of every empty professor that hath the show of religion without its fruit; for the LORD seeketh fruit, and the fruitless tree is hewn down and cast into the fire. Yet Christ turned the lesson also to faith and prayer, saying, Have faith in God, and bidding His own to believe that those things which they say shall come to pass. What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them (Mar 11:24). So the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, who curses and withers at a word, and of His Messianic office as the Judge of fruitlessness; and it teaches the church both to bring forth fruit meet for repentance and to pray in believing, unwavering faith.
webster_summary: Christ’s miracle of cursing the barren fig tree, an acted judgment on fruitlessness and a lesson of faith.
webster_full: THE WITHERED FIG TREE, Christ’s miracle of cursing a barren fig tree that then withered away.
He found the tree full of leaves but bearing no fruit.
He said, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever.
The disciples marvelled how soon it was dried up from the roots.
Christ drew from it the lesson of believing, unwavering prayer.
scriptures: And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away.
And Jesus answered and said unto it, No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever. And his disciples heard it.
And Jesus answering saith unto them, Have faith in God.
Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the modern denial of the miraculous, while its lesson of judgment on fruitless profession stands plain.
corruption_paragraphs: The withering of the fig tree has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for the Gospels join to it Christ’s own twofold lesson of judgment on fruitlessness and of believing prayer. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the only miracle of judgment among His works.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would have the tree wither by some natural blight unconnected to Christ’s word. But Mark sets word and withering together, and the disciples marvelled how soon it was dried up from the roots. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, who can curse and wither at a word, and of His Messianic office as Judge; the leafy, fruitless tree warns every empty professor that the LORD seeks fruit, not the bare show of religion, and the fruitless are hewn down. With it stands the call to faith, that what we ask, believing, we shall receive.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle of the cursed and withered fig tree, an acted judgment on barren profession.
roots_lines: The Withered Fig Tree — Christ’s miracle of cursing a barren fig tree.
The tree bore leaves but no fruit.
He said, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever.
The tree withered away from the roots.
Christ drew from it the lesson of believing prayer.
usage: As the withered fig tree warns, the LORD seeks fruit, not the bare leaves of profession.
Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever, said He to the barren tree.

word: The Coin in the Fish's Mouth
etymology: From the Latin cuneus, “wedge” or die for stamping money, naming the piece of money Christ provided for the tribute from a fish’s mouth.
biblical_def: The coin in the fish’s mouth was the miracle by which Christ provided the temple tribute for Himself and Peter, a sign of His sovereign knowledge and His command over the creatures. When they that received the tribute money asked whether His Master paid the half-shekel, Christ taught Peter that the children of the King are free, and yet, lest we should offend them (Mat 17:27), He would pay it. He bade Peter go to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when he had opened his mouth, he should find a piece of money sufficient for them both. The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for He knew that this one fish, of all the multitude of the sea, bore in its mouth the very coin, and He commanded it to Peter’s hook; such knowledge and such dominion belong to the Creator alone. It signs forth His Messianic office, for in the same breath He taught that He is the King’s own Son, free of the tribute, yet submitting to it for the sake of peace. So the miracle teaches at once the Lordship of Christ over the fish of the sea, the depth of His knowledge that searcheth all things, and the meekness of the Son of God, who, being Lord of the temple, paid its tribute rather than give needless offence, that He might fulfil all righteousness.
webster_summary: Christ’s miracle of providing the temple tribute from a coin in a fish’s mouth.
webster_full: THE COIN IN THE FISH'S MOUTH, Christ’s miracle of providing the temple tribute money.
The collectors asked whether His Master paid the tribute.
He taught that the children of the King are free, yet would not offend.
He sent Peter to the sea to take up the first fish that came.
In the fish’s mouth was a coin sufficient for them both.

And when they were come to Capernaum, they that received tribute money came to Peter, and said, Doth not your master pay tribute?

He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers?
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the modern denial of the miraculous, while its witness to His knowledge and meekness stands plain.
corruption_paragraphs: The coin in the fish’s mouth has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for Matthew records it as a plain provision of the tribute by Christ’s sovereign word. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the union of His Lordship and His meekness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would have Peter sell a fish to buy the coin, or read the saying as a figure of speech. But the LORD’s word is exact: the first fish, its mouth opened, would bear the very piece of money; and so it did. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, for His knowledge searcheth the sea and His command rules its creatures, and a sign of His Messianic office as the King’s own Son; free of the tribute, yet He paid it, that the Lord of the temple might fulfil all righteousness and give no needless offence.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle of the tribute coin from a fish’s mouth, a sign of His knowledge and His meek submission.
roots_lines: The Coin in the Fish's Mouth — Christ’s miracle of providing the temple tribute.
The collectors asked whether His Master paid the tribute.
He taught that the children of the King are free.
He sent Peter to take up the first fish from the sea.
In its mouth was a coin sufficient for them both.
usage: As Christ found the tribute in the fish’s mouth, His knowledge searcheth all things and His command rules the sea.
Lest we should offend them, said He, pay thou the tribute for Me and thee.
The King’s own Son, being free, yet paid the tribute to fulfil all righteousness.

etymology: From the place-name Gadara, the country of the Gadarenes, where the herd of swine ran headlong into the sea at Christ’s word.
biblical_def: The casting of the devils into the herd of swine was the miracle by which Christ delivered the fierce demoniac of the Gadarenes, a sign of His authority over the powers of darkness. The man dwelt among the tombs, whom no man could bind with chains; but when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped Him, and the unclean spirits cried out. When Christ demanded his name, he answered, My name is Legion: for we are many (Mar 5:9). The devils besought Him that He would send them into the swine; and He gave them leave, and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea (Mar 5:13). The man was found sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind (Mar 5:15). The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for the devils know and tremble before Him, and at His bare word a whole legion comes out; none but the Lord of heaven has such dominion over the hosts of hell. It signs forth His Messianic office, for He came to destroy the works of the devil and to set the captive free. The man, restored, was bidden to publish how great things the Lord had done for him; and the right mind given to the demoniac, set against the herd hurled into the deep, teaches that the kingdom of Christ is the casting down of Satan’s tyranny and the gracious deliverance of the souls He came to save.
webster_summary: Christ’s miracle of casting Legion out of the Gadarene demoniac into a herd of swine, proving His authority over devils.
webster_full: THE GADARENE SWINE, the herd into which Christ cast the devils named Legion.
The demoniac dwelt among the tombs, fierce and unbound.
The unclean spirits answered, My name is Legion, for we are many.
Christ gave them leave, and the herd ran into the sea and perished.
The man was found clothed, and in his right mind.

And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many.
Mar 5:13

And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea.
Mar 5:15
And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
Mar 5:19
Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed by the modern denial of the miraculous and of devils, which the eyewitness record and Christ’s authority refute.
corruption_paragraphs: The casting of Legion into the swine has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for Mark records it as a plain deliverance and a witness to Christ’s power over devils. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark His dominion over the hosts of hell.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, and with it the denial of devils, which would reduce the demoniac to a madman whose self-cure happened to frighten the herd. But the Gospel knows true unclean spirits, that confessed Christ, named themselves Legion, and at His word went out and drowned the swine; and the man was found in his right mind. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, before whom the devils tremble, and of His Messianic office; He came to destroy the works of the devil and to set the captive free, casting down Satan’s tyranny and delivering the souls He came to save.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle over the Gadarene demoniac, a sign of His authority over devils and His delivering grace.

etymology: From the Greek lepra, “scaly” or “rough,” the disease of leprosy, here cleansed at Christ’s word and touch.
biblical_def: The cleansing of the leper was the miracle in which Christ, with a touch and a word, healed the man whom the law had shut out as unclean. There came a leper to Him, kneeling down, and saying, If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean (Mar 1:40). And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth His hand, and touched him, and said, I will; be thou clean (Mat 8:3); and immediately his leprosy was cleansed. The dictionary marks this miracle as a sign of Christ’s true deity, for leprosy was held a stroke of God that none but God could heal, as it was said in Israel, Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man doth send unto me to recover a man of his leprosy? (2Ki 5:7). Yet Christ cleansed it with a word, and touched the untouchable, taking no defilement to Himself but giving cleanness to the leper; which is the very pattern of His saving work, who was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. It signs forth His Messianic office, for the cleansing of lepers was a token of the kingdom, the promised proof that the lepers are cleansed (Mat 11:5). Leprosy is a figure of sin, that defiles, spreads, and shuts out from the camp; and the willing word, I will; be thou clean, sets forth the ready grace of the Saviour who cleanses the foul sinner that comes to Him in faith.
webster_summary: Christ’s miracle of cleansing the leper with a touch and the word, I will; be thou clean.
webster_full: THE CLEANSING OF THE LEPER, Christ’s miracle of healing a man of leprosy.
The leper came kneeling, saying, If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.
Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth His hand and touched him.
He said, I will; be thou clean, and the leprosy departed.
The cleansing of lepers was a token of the kingdom of the Messiah.

And it came to pass, when the king of Israel had read the letter, that he rent his clothes, and said, Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man doth send unto me to recover a man of his leprosy? wherefore consider, I pray you, and see how he seeketh a quarrel against me.
corruption_summary: A miracle of Christ; assailed only by the modern denial of the miraculous, while its witness to His cleansing grace stands plain.
corruption_paragraphs: The cleansing of the leper has drawn little redefinition in its meaning, for the Gospels record it as a plain healing and a token of the Messianic kingdom. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the willing word of the Saviour to the defiled.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption it meets is the broad modern denial of the miraculous, which would have the man recovering by natural remission and crediting it to Christ. But the text is plain: He put forth His hand, touched the leper, said, I will; be thou clean, and immediately the leprosy was cleansed. The principle to recover is that the miracle is a sign of Christ’s true deity, for in Israel none but God could recover a man of his leprosy, and a sign of His Messianic office, for the cleansing of lepers was the promised token of His coming; and leprosy being a figure of sin, the willing word sets forth the ready grace of Him who cleanses every sinner that comes to Him in faith.
roots_summary: Christ’s miracle of cleansing the leper, a sign of His deity and of His ready grace to the defiled.
